title: Flipping Bits
directAnswer: Flip every one of the 32 bits of an unsigned integer. XOR with a 32-bit all-ones mask: n ^ 0xFFFFFFFF turns every 0 into 1 and every 1 into 0. Equivalently it equals 4294967295 − n, since flipping all bits of a value below the all-ones ceiling is just subtracting it from that ceiling. It is O(1) — no loop.

remember.formula:
return n ^ 0xFFFFFFFF        # flip the low 32 bits
# equivalently: 4294967295 - n
# equivalently: ~n & 0xFFFFFFFF
rules: **XOR with 1 flips a bit; XOR with 0 leaves it.** A mask of all 1s (0xFFFFFFFF) flips every one of the 32 bits at once.
The mask is **exactly 32 ones** = `0xFFFFFFFF` = `4294967295`. Use this width — not 31, not 64.
**4294967295 − n gives the same answer** because no borrow ever happens: all-ones minus any 32-bit value is its bitwise complement.
In languages with infinite-width integers (Python) you **must mask** `~n & 0xFFFFFFFF` — bare `~n` produces a negative number with infinite leading 1s.
In Java use a **long** (`0xFFFFFFFFL`) so the result fits the unsigned 32-bit range without sign issues.
whenToUse: Compute the bitwise complement within a fixed bit width
Toggle a known set of bits in one operation via XOR
Translate 'unsigned NOT' into a masked operation
antiSignals: You need to flip only some bits → XOR with a targeted mask, not all ones
Width is not fixed / arbitrary precision → define the mask explicitly each time
You need to count or locate set bits → popcount, not inversion
Signed two's-complement semantics required → be careful, plain ~ may suffice
remember.takeaway: Flipping all bits in a fixed width is one XOR with an all-ones mask of that width. Remember 0xFFFFFFFF = 4294967295, mask in Python, and use long in Java — then it's a single O(1) operation, no per-bit loop.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know XOR with 1 toggles a bit and can build a 32-bit all-ones mask, plus the language gotchas: masking ~n in Python and using an unsigned-safe type in Java.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning bare ~n in Python (a negative, infinitely-wide number) without the & 0xFFFFFFFF mask, or using a 32-bit signed int in Java so the high bit makes the result negative.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Give the one-line XOR-with-mask answer, mention the 4294967295 − n equivalence and why it holds, and call out the masking/typing requirement for the language you're in.

problemStatement: You are given a list of 32-bit **unsigned** integers. For each integer `n`, flip all 32 of its bits (turn every 1 into a 0 and every 0 into a 1) and return the resulting unsigned decimal value.
constraints: All 32 bits are flipped, including leading zeros
The result is interpreted as an unsigned 32-bit value
understanding: An unsigned 32-bit number has exactly 32 bit positions, many of which may be leading zeros. Flipping means inverting all 32 of them — leading zeros become leading ones. The all-ones 32-bit pattern is 0xFFFFFFFF = 4294967295, and inverting n is the same as XORing it against that pattern, or subtracting n from it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are we flipping all 32 bits, including leading zeros?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Even if n is small, its high bits are zeros that must become ones. The result is taken over the full 32-bit width.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the value signed or unsigned?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Unsigned. The flipped result can exceed 2³¹, so in Java you need a long, and in Python you mask to keep it within 32 bits.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why does 4294967295 − n give the same answer?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 0xFFFFFFFF is all ones. Subtracting any 32-bit value from all ones never borrows, so each bit independently becomes its complement — identical to XOR with the mask.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What's the trap with ~n in Python?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Python ints are arbitrary precision, so ~n is −(n+1) with infinite leading ones. You must mask: ~n & 0xFFFFFFFF.

examples.explanation: 2147483647 = 0x7FFFFFFF (low 31 bits set). Flipping gives 0x80000000 = 2147483648 — only the top bit is now set.
1 = 0x00000001. Flipping gives 0xFFFFFFFE = 4294967294 — all bits set except the lowest.
All 32 zeros flip to all ones: 0xFFFFFFFF = 4294967295.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree. Flipping Bits is the 'invert a fixed width' branch — one XOR with an all-ones mask.

approaches.name: Bit-by-Bit Loop — Toggle Each Position
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the explicit, teaching version, then collapse all 32 steps into one masked operation.
hints: Walk the 32 bit positions. For each position i, read bit (n >> i) & 1.
If that bit is 0, set the corresponding bit in the result; if it's 1, leave the result's bit as 0.
After 32 iterations the result holds the flipped value. It's constant time (32 is fixed) but verbose.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Exactly 32 iterations regardless of n, each doing constant bit work — O(1) time and O(1) space, just with a large constant factor.
approaches.explanation:
Invert the number one position at a time to make the mechanics explicit.

**The per-bit logic.** For each of the 32 positions, extract the bit with `(n >> i) & 1`. Flipping means: a 0 should become a 1, and a 1 should become a 0. So whenever the extracted bit is 0, set bit `i` in the result with `result |= (1L << i)`; whenever it is 1, do nothing (the result bit is already 0).

**Why 32 positions exactly.** The value is an unsigned 32-bit integer, so there are precisely 32 bits to consider — including the leading zeros of a small number, which must flip to ones. Looping `i` from 0 to 31 covers them all.

**Why this is correct but clunky.** It produces the right answer and runs in constant time (32 is a fixed bound), but it spells out by hand what a single XOR does atomically. Every one of those 32 conditional sets is just 'toggle this bit', which is exactly XOR with 1. Recognising that lets you replace the entire loop with one masked operation.
approaches.insight: Each loop step is 'flip bit i' — and flipping a bit is XOR with 1. Thirty-two such flips at once is XOR with thirty-two 1s, i.e. 0xFFFFFFFF. The loop is the unrolled form of the optimal one-liner.

dryRun.intro: Inspect each of the low bits; flip 0s to 1s, leave 1s as 0.

java.explanation: Shift bit i down to the ones place and isolate it with & 1.
If the original bit was 0, set bit i of the result — the actual flip.

python.explanation: Set the result's bit i when the source bit was 0.

diagrams.title: Toggling positions one at a time
diagrams.caption: Each bit is inspected and flipped — the loop unrolls the single XOR below.

pitfalls: Looping only 31 times or up to the highest set bit — leading zeros must flip too.
Using (1 << i) on a 32-bit int in Java and overflowing the sign bit — use 1L << i.
Writing the loop at all when one XOR does the whole job.

approaches.name: XOR with All-Ones Mask (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Say 'XOR with 0xFFFFFFFF flips all 32 bits in one step'.
hints: XOR with 1 flips a bit; XOR with 0 leaves it. To flip all 32 bits, XOR against 32 ones.
Thirty-two ones is the constant 0xFFFFFFFF = 4294967295. So the answer is n ^ 0xFFFFFFFF.
Mind the language: in Python mask with & 0xFFFFFFFF if you use ~n; in Java use a long literal 0xFFFFFFFFL.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single XOR (or subtraction) — one machine operation, no loop, no allocation. O(1) time and space.
approaches.explanation:
Replace the 32-step loop with one masked operation.

**Why XOR with all ones flips everything.** XOR is the 'toggle if the mask bit is 1' operator: `b ^ 1` is the opposite of `b`, and `b ^ 0` is `b` unchanged. A mask of all ones therefore toggles every bit simultaneously. For 32 bits the all-ones mask is `0xFFFFFFFF`, so `n ^ 0xFFFFFFFF` is the full bitwise inversion in one shot.

**The subtraction equivalence.** Because `0xFFFFFFFF` is all ones, subtracting any 32-bit `n` from it never triggers a borrow — at every position you compute `1 − bit`, which is exactly the complement of that bit. So `4294967295 − n` produces the identical result. Either form is fine; the XOR makes the intent (flip bits) clearer.

**The Python gotcha.** Python integers are arbitrary precision, so the built-in `~n` returns `−(n + 1)` — a negative number with infinitely many leading ones, not a 32-bit value. To get the unsigned 32-bit complement you must mask: `~n & 0xFFFFFFFF`, or just use `n ^ 0xFFFFFFFF` which is already bounded.

**The Java gotcha.** A 32-bit signed `int` would interpret a flipped result with its top bit set as negative. Use a `long` and the literal `0xFFFFFFFFL` so the value stays in the unsigned 32-bit range `[0, 4294967295]`.
approaches.insight: Flipping a fixed-width number is one XOR with an all-ones mask of that width — and that equals subtracting it from the all-ones ceiling. The only real work is getting the width and the language's integer semantics right.

dryRun.intro: XOR every zero bit against a one to flip it.

code.python:
def flippingBits(n: int) -> int:
    return n ^ 0xFFFFFFFF      # flip all 32 bits; mask keeps it in range

java.explanation: XOR against 32 ones toggles every bit; the L makes it a long so the high bit doesn't go negative.

python.explanation: XOR with the 32-bit all-ones mask flips every bit and bounds the result to 32 bits.

diagrams.title: One XOR flips all 32 bits
diagrams.caption: The mask is 32 ones; XOR toggles each position at once.

edgeCases.behavior: 0 ^ 0xFFFFFFFF = 4294967295 — all zeros flip to all ones.
0xFFFFFFFF ^ 0xFFFFFFFF = 0 — all ones flip to all zeros.
0x80000000 ^ 0xFFFFFFFF = 0x7FFFFFFF = 2147483647 — only the top bit was set, now cleared.

pitfalls: Returning bare ~n in Python — gives a negative, infinite-width number instead of the 32-bit complement.
Using a signed 32-bit int in Java so the flipped value reads as negative — use long with 0xFFFFFFFFL.
Masking with the wrong width (0xFFFF or 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF) and flipping too few or too many bits.

commonMistakes: Returning bare ~n in Python without masking to 32 bits.
Using a signed 32-bit int in Java, making the result negative when the top bit is set.
Flipping only the significant bits and ignoring leading zeros.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Unmasked complement in Python
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Python ints are arbitrary precision, so ~n = −(n+1) with infinite leading ones — not a 32-bit unsigned value.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Signed int in Java
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A 32-bit int treats a result with the high bit set as negative. Use a long and the L-suffixed mask.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int result = (int) n ^ 0xFFFFFFFF;   // can be negative

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong mask width
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Flipping 32 bits needs exactly 32 ones. A 16-bit or 64-bit mask flips the wrong number of positions.

followupVariations.hint: Count set bits instead of flipping them — popcount via n & (n − 1).

patternNote: Fixed-width bitwise complement. To invert all bits within a known width, XOR with an all-ones mask of that width (0xFFFFFFFF for 32 bits), which also equals subtracting from the all-ones ceiling. The recurring subtlety is integer width and signedness, not the algorithm.
